title: SYSK Gets Weird Playlist: Mermaids: Not a real thing
summary: Gets Weird playlist episode (episode three) of Stuff You Should Know, titled "Mermaids: Not a Real Thing." The hosts open with banter about Splash, Neil Young, and the Ramones, then cover mermaid mythology and lore: the Kiryat Yam (Israel) mermaid reward and 2009 photo, Babylonian Ea and Poseidon/Neptune, Pliny the Elder's Nereids and sea men, Hans Christian Andersen's Little Mermaid versus Disney, the Syrian goddess Atargatis, the German Nix river-dweller, West African Mami Wata, and the duality of mermaid myths. They discuss sirens versus mermaids, eyewitness accounts (Kai Islands WWII monster, John Smith, Henry Hudson, Columbus and possible manatee sightings), and Carl Bantz's 1990 tongue-in-cheek Limnology and Oceanography article on extinct mermaids. They then cover the 1830 Scottish Benbecula mermaid, the Discovery/Animal Planet mockumentary Mermaids: The Body Found and its sequel with fake marine geologist Torsten Schmidt and NOAA's statement, a 1430 Edam mermaid story, and professional mermaid shows at Weeki Wachee Springs in Florida. The episode closes with a request for iTunes reviews and jingle submissions.

segments.title: Gets Weird playlist introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Gets Weird playlist, episode three, on mermaids.

segments.title: Opening banter about Splash and music
segments.summary: The hosts open with the standard show intro, then chat about the movie Splash, Eugene Levy, Daryl Hannah, Neil Young, and Billy Joel.

segments.title: Banter on musicians and the Ramones
segments.summary: Discussion of musicians phoning in reunion shows, the Police reunion, and a Rolling Stone article about the Ramones.

segments.title: Mermaid sightings are fake and time-machine joke
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode's premise that mermaids are not real and the lore is the focus. The hosts joke about bringing doctored photos back in time to sell them.

segments.title: Kiryat Yam mermaid reward
segments.summary: The town of Kiryat Yam on Israel's coast offers a million dollars for incontrovertible evidence of a mermaid. A 2009 photo shows a mermaid on a rock, and the town's offer is compared to Loch Ness tourism.

segments.title: Mermaid mythology: Ea, Poseidon, and Pliny's Nereids
segments.summary: The hosts discuss mythology and misogyny in mermaid folklore, then Pliny the Elder's Natural History describing Nereids and sea men, and the Babylonian sea god Ea as a predecessor of Poseidon and Neptune.

segments.title: The original Little Mermaid story
segments.summary: Chuck summarizes Hans Christian Andersen's darker original Little Mermaid, in which she fails to kill the prince, turns to sea foam, and may earn a soul by helping humans for 300 years.

segments.title: Sea men climbing onto ships and mermaid appearance
segments.summary: Pliny describes sea men climbing onto ships at night. The hosts describe the typical mermaid as a woman's upper body with a fish tail, and note that some legends describe ugly mermaids.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Break in the episode with a short band-name style interlude and a return to the topic.

segments.title: Sirens versus mermaids and beauty
segments.summary: Mermaids are often beautiful and lure sailors, sometimes with singing. Sirens are half bird and differ from mermaids. The hosts digress into celebrity singers.

segments.title: Atargatis, the Syrian mermaid goddess
segments.summary: The hosts recount Atargatis from around 1000 BCE in Syria, a protector goddess who loved a human man, accidentally killed him, and became a mermaid after throwing herself into a lake.

segments.title: German Nix and West African Mami Wata
segments.summary: Germany's river-dwelling Nix lure men to drown. Mami Wata from West Africa is nurturing but murderous if crossed, and the hosts discuss duality in mythic creatures.

segments.title: Hybrid mythological creatures and bestiality theory
segments.summary: The hosts compare mermaids to other hybrid creatures like sirens, the minotaur, and centaurs. Chuck mentions scholars who link hybrid myths to lax attitudes about bestiality, and the hosts discuss the documentary Zoo.

segments.title: Eyewitness accounts: Kai Islands, John Smith, Columbus
segments.summary: A WWII-era monster with webbed hands and feet on Indonesia's Kai Islands, and mermaid claims from John Smith and Henry Hudson. Columbus's diary describes three mermaids not as pretty as depicted, which may have been manatees.

segments.title: Why people saw mermaids: suggestibility and mistaken identity
segments.summary: Explanations include hallucination from long voyages and suggestibility, since people believed mermaids existed during the Age of Exploration. The hosts reference the earlier sea monsters episode.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break.

segments.title: Carl Bantz's 1990 article on extinct mermaids
segments.summary: Carl Bantz's 1990 tongue-in-cheek but straight-faced article in Limnology and Oceanography describes mermaids as an extinct species with horny skinfolds, warm-water habitat, and extinction by jellyfish stings. The hosts also cover a 1830 Benbecula, Scotland mermaid that was killed by a thrown rock and given a funeral.

segments.title: Mermaids mockumentary and Torsten Schmidt hoax
segments.summary: Animal Planet aired a mockumentary about mermaids that drew big ratings and led to a sequel. NOAA issued a statement saying mermaids do not exist. The fake marine geologist Torsten Schmidt appeared in footage of a webbed hand striking a sub window; the hosts note the actor resembled Zach Galifianakis.

segments.title: Edam mermaid story from 1430
segments.summary: A story of two girls in Edam who supposedly found a mermaid, dressed it as a girl, and taught it to live on land, where it stayed mute. The hosts suggest it may have been a person with a physical deformation, similar to freak show acts.

segments.title: Professional mermaids and Weeki Wachee Springs
segments.summary: Weeki Wachee Springs in Florida drew big crowds with mermaid shows in the 1940s to 1960s, including Elvis Presley and Don Knotts. Professional mermaids train for years, use the mermaid crawl, and some use their platform for ocean ecology advocacy.

segments.title: Listener request and sign-off
segments.summary: In place of listener mail, the hosts ask listeners to leave iTunes reviews, tell a friend, and submit jingles. They close with social media and website contact information.
